title: 'It's Essentially Been One Long Day': Daughter Searches for Parents After Nepal Floods
summary:
Shreya Ahuja, a 30-year-old physician from North Carolina, had spoken to her parents just hours before devastating floods struck Nepal. They had completed a pilgrimage trek to Mount Kailash and were heading toward the border. The next morning, she saw messages about flash flooding and tried to reach them.

"I tried texting them. I tried calling them. And initially, I wasn't too concerned," Ahuja told NPR's Morning Edition. "I feel like everyone thinks, what are the chances that they were in that exact spot?"

As of Friday, police in Nepal reported more than 500 deaths on the Nepal side of the border, with over 1,500 people still missing after nearly 30-foot-high waves raced down a river between Tibet and Nepal. Ahuja's parents, Deepak and Madhu Ahuja, are U.S. citizens and small business owners in Dallas. They were making the pilgrimage for her father's 60th birthday.

Their last known location was the Gyirong border crossing between China and Nepal. CCTV footage shows the flooding destroying the building where their group was supposed to be. Ahuja is now in Washington, D.C., with family, including her grandparents.

"It's essentially been one long day. Haven't really slept," she told NPR's Steve Inskeep. "We're just really hoping that we can get to them in time."

Ahuja is calling for more collaboration among India, Nepal, China, and the United States. She also wants Starlink to be authorized in Nepal, saying friends who work with SpaceX told her the company had tried to deploy dishes but hadn't received approval. "These are all tangible things that could really help us get into contact with people on the ground," she said.

The search continues, and her family holds onto hope.
why_it_matters: This story shows how a single fast-moving climate disaster can cross borders, and how access to communication can be just as important as rescue teams. It also exposes the gaps between countries and companies in preparing for emergencies.

background_read: Nepal (a mountainous country in South Asia, sandwiched between China and India) experiences dangerous flash flooding every year, especially during monsoon season, when heavy rain quickly turns rivers into walls of water; such floods can arrive in minutes.

The border region described in the article is part of the Himalayas, where narrow valleys and damaged roads make search efforts slow; Mount Kailash (a mountain in Tibet considered sacred by Hindus, Buddhists, and Jains) draws pilgrims from across the region.
Ahuja's parents, who own a small business in Dallas, were returning from this type of pilgrimage when the disaster struck the Gyirong border crossing between China and Nepal.

Her request to bring Starlink—a satellite internet system operated by SpaceX—into Nepal highlights a key problem: cell towers and internet often fail in remote disaster zones, leaving rescue teams and families unconnected.

International disasters on shared borders also create coordination problems, because countries must agree on who searches where and how to share information before they can act quickly; that is why Ahuja is calling for more collaboration among India, Nepal, China, and the United States.

perspectives.description: Ahuja's call for collaboration among India, Nepal, China, and the U.S. points to a practical solution: disasters do not respect borders, so rescue efforts should not either. Satellite internet like Starlink could quickly connect isolated areas and speed up search operations.

The delayed approval for Starlink is a frustrating example of paperwork slowing down a life-saving tool. The enormous number of missing people shows how weak communication infrastructure can leave families in the dark during the most urgent hours.

The disaster reveals a repeating pattern in mountain regions: flash floods strike suddenly, and remote terrain makes search-and-rescue extremely slow. When roads, phones, and CCTV all fail, even families with resources and American citizenship can be left waiting.

If search efforts succeed, there may be new pressure on Nepal to authorize emergency satellite systems and improve cross-border disaster plans. If they do not, advocates will likely demand earlier warnings and better coordination before the next flood season.
